title: Melania: the series review – so bad it robbed me of my capacity to discern time and space
text:
Previously on Melania: earlier this year – either because it found her a compelling subject, or because it wanted to flatter the president before a potentially destructive upcoming antitrust trial – Amazon spent $75m (£57m) to make and market a theatrically released documentary about Melania Trump.
I’m telling you this for two reasons. First, because you didn’t watch the Melania film. Nobody did, except for journalists who sat in otherwise empty cinemas and (if reports are to believed) people who responded to Craigslist ads offering them $50 to see it. The second reason is because Melania is a series now.
And, listen, I tried. I really tried to go into the series with an open mind. The first rule of criticism is that you should review what something is, and not what you want it to be. I was unable to do this, because I wanted it to be watchable, or to have any form of identifiable substance. In both cases, Melania came up wildly short.
Even calling it a series requires a wild stretching of the imagination. What we actually have here are two episodes, neither of which make it to the 40-minute mark, consisting of nothing but junky little offcuts that fail to tell us anything about anything. A lot of these episodes consist of Melania Trump flatly intoning the sort of empty platitudes found on AI-written CVs. For example, she understands that “meaningful action is driven by change”, which I’m sure will be a great relief to us all.
What a legitimately bizarre thing this is. Even its presentation is weird. Both episodes are full of the sort of faux-lifestyle shaky 8mm footage you’d expect to find on something like With Love, Meghan. It’s a trope you see when someone wants to inject a sense of homemade glamour into proceedings, except here a lot of this cutesy footage is actually of Arlington National Cemetery, home to thousands of dead American soldiers.
Then – and I promise that this isn’t an exaggeration – there is a sequence in the first episode where Melania deliberates about the exact placement of a brooch. This sequence goes on for so much longer than you would expect it to. While it was on, and she was agonising over the exact millimetre position of the brooch, I put the episode on 1.5x speed, and it still took for ever to finish. I ended up falling into a catatonic fugue state, watching it. I might still be watching it now. The show has robbed me of my capacity to discern the boundaries of time and space.
In truth, there is a single grain of substance here. The second episode sees Melania travel to North Carolina and California to meet victims of Hurricane Helene and the wildfires. When the camera pans around to hear the stories of the people who lost their homes, the series momentarily becomes human.
But that doesn’t last long, because it turns out that this was simply used as a way to leapfrog into a discussion about Melania’s work with foster children. Inevitably, her contribution to this involves saying the name of her website out loud in full, twice, then wanging on about the blockchain. Everything unstoppably, inevitably, goes back to her. At one point, the first assistant director shows Melania how his brother’s house was affected by the California fires. “This is all he packed,” he tells her sadly as he swipes through photos on his phone. “His guitars and his Maga hats.”
Calling Melania thin gruel would be an insult to the gruel industry. There are times when even the interviewer palpably gives up. He asks Melania how she unwinds, leading with a base-pleasing question about whether or not she prays. She shrugs it off with some woolly talk about how God is inside us. Does she go for long walks? “I don’t.” Instead, she reveals, she just goes to the spa a lot. “The first priority is to take care of yourself, so you can take care of other people,” she tells us, exactly as someone who tends not to care about other people very much would say. The exchange is Melania in microcosm.
But you’re not going to watch this either. Why would you? Melania is a dead-eyed advert that barely manages to masquerade as entertainment. It will leave you bored and depressed in equal measure. But, hey, so long as it helps with the antitrust trial.
